questions.question: Examine the effectiveness of fear appeals in persuasion. Under what conditions are they most effective? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Examine the effectiveness of fear appeals in persuasion. Under what conditions are they most
  • effective?
  • Fear appeals are persuasive messages that arouse fear to motivate attitude or behaviour change (e.g.,
  • anti-smoking or road-safety campaigns).
  • Effectiveness:
  • • Research shows that fear appeals can increase persuasion when they produce moderate fear
  • and when individuals see a clear, achievable way to reduce the threat.
  • • Strong fear without guidance creates anxiety and leads to defensive avoidance (“It won’t
  • happen to me”).
  • Most effective when 1. Moderate, not extreme fear.
  • The message must be alarming enough to draw attention but not paralyzing. 2. Availability of an effective
  • solution. 3. The audience must perceive a recommended action that clearly removes or reduces the
  • danger. 4. Perceived personal susceptibility.
  • The message should convince people that the threat applies to them, not just others. 5. Credibility of the
  • communicator. Fear appeals from trustworthy experts (doctors, traffic authorities) are more persuasive. 6.
  • Audience characteristics.
  • Individuals high in self-efficacy respond better; low self-esteem audiences may resist or deny the
  • message.
  • Fear appeals work best when combined with constructive information (“danger + safety message”)—in
  • essence, arousing fear but also providing hope and control.

  • influence real-world events without logical cause (“If I
  • wear my lucky charm, I’ll succeed”).
  • Cognitive
  • basis
  • Arises from rational reasoning extended beyond
  • facts; involves mental simulation of “what might
  • have been.”
  • Arises from emotional and associative thinking; violates
  • logical or scientific causation.
  • FunctionCan motivate improvement (upward thinking) orprovide comfort (downward thinking). Offers psychological comfort by creating illusion ofcontrol.
  • Potential errorProduces guilt, regret, or unrealistic beliefs aboutcontrol over uncontrollable outcomes. Leads to irrational fear, superstition, avoidance, or falsecausal links.
  • Example in
  • daily life
  • Survivor guilt after accident: “If I had taken a later
  • bus, it wouldn’t have happened.”
  • Refusing to eat chocolate shaped like insects; believing it
  • shares the same properties.
  • Comparison: Both reflect the human tendency to impose order and meaning on events. Counterfactual
  • thinking uses logical structure but misapplies causation to the past; magical thinking breaks rational links
  • altogether. Each shows the limits of human cognition under emotion or uncertainty.

questions.question: Define diffusion of responsibility and bystander effect. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Define diffusion of responsibility and bystander effect.
  • A. Diffusion of responsibility: A phenomenon where individuals feel less personal responsibility for
  • taking action when others are present. Responsibility for helping is “diffused” across all bystanders,
  • leading each to assume someone else will act. Here witnesses assume someone else will take charge, and
  • pluralistic ignorance, where people misinterpret the calm demeanor of others as a sign that no crisis
  • exists. Research initiated by Darley and Latané demonstrates that as group size increases, personal
  • accountability diminishes, a pattern that extends beyond physical locations into online environments and
  • workplace hierarchies. However, the sources also highlight that prosocial priming—activating helpful
  • concepts in a person's mind—and clear communication can effectively counteract this apathy. By
  • assigning specific roles and fostering a shared sense of identity, organizations and individuals can bypass
  • social inhibition to promote decisive, life-saving action.
  • Bystander effect: A social phenomenon where the likelihood of helping decreases as the number of
  • bystanders increases. Discovered by Darley and Latané (1970) after the Kitty Genovese case, it occurs
  • through a sequence: failure to notice, misinterpretation, diffusion of responsibility, and evaluating
  • personal risk. Research consistently shows that as the number of bystanders increases, the likelihood of
  • any single person intervening decreases. The concept was famously studied by psychologists John Darley
  • and Bibb Latané In their foundational 1968 experiment, they found that 85% of participants sought help
  • when they believed they were the lone witness to a peer's seizure, but that figure plummeted to 31% when
  • they believed four other bystanders were present.
  • The effect is primarily driven by three psychological processes: 1. Diffusion of Responsibility: In a group,
  • the sense of personal obligation is diluted because individuals assume someone else will take action. 2.
  • Pluralistic Ignorance: Witnesses often look to the reactions of others to gauge the severity of a situation;
  • if no one else reacts, they may conclude it is not a true emergency. 3. Evaluation Apprehension:
  • Individuals may hesitate to help due to a fear of being judged or appearing foolish to others. The effect
  • can be reduced through 1. Direct Requests: Pointing to a specific person and giving a clear instruction
  • (e.g., "You in the red shirt, call 911") forces that individual to take responsibility. 2. Training: Programs
  • like first-aid training educate people on how to overcome barriers to helping and 3.Prosocial Priming:
  • Research suggests that activating altruistic concepts in a person's mind before a request can minimize the
  • bystander effect, even in online contexts
